- **What the labels mean** (a tiny table: Public / Internal / Confidential / Highly Confidential + a one-line "use when…").
- **What happens automatically** (reassure: some labels apply themselves; sharing limits are guardrails, not punishments).
- **Where to get help** (link/contact). 
Tone: warm, zero jargon, no acronyms unexpanded. Imagine A's busiest team member reading it in 60 seconds.

### 3. Reply to A's email (you are "B," A is the sender)
A is stressed, capacity-constrained, thinks their current system works, fears added steps/learning curve/lost efficiency. **Do NOT** dismiss or over-explain. This is the Openness + Inclusiveness test.
- **Acknowledge genuinely** — their time pressure is real and valid.
- **Reframe** — this isn't a new filing system replacing theirs; it's a lightweight layer, much of it automatic, designed to *reduce* risk and overshare-anxiety.
- **Concede honestly** (Calibration) — yes there's a small learning curve; here's how we're minimizing it (defaults/auto-classification, a 1-page guide, no workflow rebuild).
- **Offer partnership** — invite their team into the pilot so the rollout fits how they actually work; ask for their input. (Inclusiveness — and it converts a skeptic into a stakeholder.)
- **Stay warm, direct, brief.** Sign as B. ~150–200 words.

### 4. AI-usage writeup (≤200 words)
Be specific and honest — this itself is scored as judgment. Cover: model(s) used (Claude / Claude Code), the tasks where it helped most (research on Google's actual label/DLP/AI-classification mechanics; structuring the plan; pressure-testing the AI-classification tradeoff; tightening prose), and the guidance/context YOU gave it (the real feature set, the 5-hr scope constraint, CG's Operating Values, the instruction to keep final language your own). The honest "I directed it here, I overrode it there, I wrote the prose myself" narrative reads as exactly the judgment they want.

## Assumptions to state up front (Calibration in action)
You're writing without real context, so declare it: org headcount/structure unknown (assume ~100–200 staff, mostly knowledge workers on Google Workspace); assume Enterprise Standard or Plus edition; assume Legal/Compliance exists to own taxonomy + retention; assume no existing label taxonomy; assume remote-first workforce; assume modest IT team (you + consultants). Note how each would change the plan if wrong (e.g., "if we're on Business Standard, AI classification is off the table entirely and Phase 2 becomes a manual backlog effort").

## Time budget (5 hours)
- 0:30 — re-read, lock assumptions, sketch all four outlines.
- 1:45 — deployment plan (the heaviest piece).
- 1:00 — user guide.
- 0:30 — email reply.
- 0:30 — AI writeup + assumptions/uncertainties section.
- 0:45 — tighten to ≤6 pages, de-AI pass, proofread, strip identifying info, export PDF.
If you run over, STOP at 5:00, note it, and flag where you got to (their policy rewards honesty here).

## Point-losers to avoid
- Going over 6 pages (9 is a hard "won't read past this").
- Putting your name anywhere, including the PDF filename.
- Designing a giant taxonomy (shows poor scope judgment — small and governed wins).
- Putting AI-model training on the critical path to Jan.
- Generic LLM prose — they explicitly penalize it. Run the de-AI pass; no em dashes; your voice.
- Steamrolling A in the email.
- Forgetting the outside-IT dependencies question and the success-criteria question.

## How we'll work (honest division of labor)
- I did the research above (sanctioned LLM use — discloseable in deliverable #4).
- YOU write the prose and make the calls; final language is yours.
- Hand me each draft and I'll pressure-test it hard (gaps, weak spots, value-alignment, page budget) — that critique loop is where we make it excellent.

9	Fact-checkable research brief for the Coefficient Giving work test. Every nontrivial claim has an inline URL so Alex can verify it. Confidence flags: **[H]** high (primary Google/MS docs), **[M]** medium (consultancy/vendor), **[L]** low/unverified. A "⚠ version-dependent / sources disagree" list is at the end. Compiled from a 4-agent deep-research run, 2026-06-02.
10	
11	# Part 1 — Google Workspace / Drive classification labels (the mechanics)
12	
13	## What they are
14	Classification labels are **metadata applied to Drive files and Gmail messages** to help organize, find, and apply policy to content. They can be a simple tag or carry structured fields. **[H]** ([Google: get started as a labels admin](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/get-started-as-a-classification-labels-admin)). Managed in the **Label Manager** (Admin console → Security → Access and data control → Label manager, or drive.google.com/labels). **[H]** ([Workspace Updates 2024-07](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2024/07/enable-classification-labels-on-workspace-apps.html))
15	
16	## Badged vs. standard labels (CORRECTED — important)
17	- A **badge list field** is a field type ("pick one from a list of badges") that renders the selected value as a **colored rectangle** in Docs/Sheets/Slides/Drive — a visible handling reminder. Only **one badge list field per label**. **[H]** ([Google: create classification labels](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-classification-labels-for-your-organization))
18	- **The old "one badged label per organization" rule has been relaxed.** Google's 2021 launch post said one per company ([Workspace Updates 2021-12](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2021/12/enhanced-content-classification.html)), but current docs say up to **150 labels per org, "including multiple badged labels."** The constraint is now one badge *field* per label, not one badged label per org. **[H, but the change was never explicitly announced — verify in your console if it matters]**
19	- As of a **Nov 2025** update, badge values display in Drive list/grid views (highest-ranked badged label shows; a count icon flags additional labels). **[H]** ([Workspace Updates 2025-11](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/11/data-classification-labels-visible-google-drive.html))
20	- Admins can attach a **"learn more" documentation link** to a badge field; users see it on hover or in the Labels pane. **[H]** (create-labels page above)
21	
22	## Editions (who can do what)
23	- **Create + manually apply labels**: Frontline Starter/Standard/Plus, Business Standard/Plus, all Enterprise editions, Education Standard/Plus, Essentials tiers. **Excluded**: Business Starter, Education Fundamentals (for manual apply). **[H]** (get-started page)
24	- **DLP-driven auto-labeling**: requires Frontline Standard/Plus, **Enterprise Standard/Plus**, Education Fundamentals/Standard/Plus, Enterprise Essentials Plus (+ Cloud Identity Premium). **Business Standard/Plus can create and manually apply labels but CANNOT auto-apply them via DLP.** **[H]** ([Google: DLP for Drive rules](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-dlp-for-drive-rules-and-custom-content-detectors))
25	- **AI classification**: see Part 2.
26	
27	## Limits (verbatim from Google docs) **[H]**
28	| Limit | Value |
29	|---|---|
30	| Labels per org | 150 (incl. badged) |
31	| Fields per label | 10 |
32	| Options per field | 200 |
33	| Labels a *user* can apply to one file | 5 |
34	| Total labels on a file (user + rule-applied) | 20 |
35	| Total labels on a Gmail message | 20 |
36	| Text field length | 100 chars |
37	| AI classification models per org | 5 |
38	Source: [create-labels](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-classification-labels-for-your-organization) + [get-started](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/get-started-as-a-classification-labels-admin). **Field types are immutable after publishing.**
39	
40	## The three ways labels get applied
41	1. **Manual** — user right-clicks a Drive file → Labels → Apply (or File → Labels in Docs). Bulk apply up to 100 files. Needs edit access + "can apply" permission. **[H]** ([apply labels in Drive](https://support.google.com/drive/answer/13495216))
42	2. **Default classification** — auto-applies a label to **new** files (or on ownership change) scoped to an OU/group. **Does NOT retroactively label existing files. Only supports labels with an options-list field** (not badge/text/number/date/person). **[H]** ([default classification](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/apply-default-classification-labels-to-new-files-automatically))
43	3. **Rule-based (DLP)** and **AI classification** — see below.
44	
45	## DLP integration, sharing controls, locking, retention
46	- **DLP auto-labeling**: a DLP-for-Drive rule scans content (predefined detectors for SSNs/credit cards/etc., custom word lists, regex, likelihood thresholds) and, on match, applies a label + a single-select options value. DLP label actions support **single-select options list fields only**. **[H]** (DLP-for-Drive page above)
47	- **Label-driven sharing controls**: a DLP rule's actions can **block external sharing** and **disable download/print/copy** (for commenters/viewers; editors unaffected) alongside applying a label. **[H]**
48	  - ⚠ Side effect: once any sharing-blocking DLP rule is active, external users can't view version history of **any** file that ever had **any** DLP rule applied — including label-only rules. **[H]** ([DLP for Drive FAQ](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/dlp-for-drive-faq))
49	  - There's no confirmed mechanism for a label to restrict sharing **on its own** without a DLP rule. **[L]**
50	- **Label locking**: labels/fields/options used by an active DLP, Vault retention, default-classification, or AI rule are **locked** — can't be disabled or deleted (renaming and adding options still allowed). Unlock by removing from all rules. **[H]** (create-labels + DLP pages)
51	- **Vault retention**: retention rules can key off a label's **date field** (since Jun 2023); litigation holds override retention. **[H]** ([Vault Drive retention](https://support.google.com/vault/answer/4388708)); whether non-date field values can trigger retention is **[M]**.
52	- **Audit**: Drive audit logs record label/DLP events (e.g. "DLP Rule applied Label Contract"); DLP rules support **"audit only"** mode for testing; the Security Investigation Tool inspects rule triggers. **[H]**
53	
54	## Priority order when methods conflict (CORRECTED — it's 5 levels, not 3)
55	Verbatim hierarchy, highest wins: **(1) DLP without user-overwrite → (2) manual/user-applied → (3) DLP with user-overwrite → (4) AI classification → (5) default classification.** **[H]** ([AI classification page](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/label-google-drive-files-automatically-using-ai-classification)). Plain version: DLP beats AI beats default; manual user labels beat AI. Multi-DLP-rule ties break by **options-list order** (higher option wins), not rule number. **[H]**
56	
57	# Part 2 — Google's AI classification for Drive labels
58	
59	## What it actually is (key nuance)
60	The **generally-available** "AI classification" uses **custom models trained on YOUR org's own labeled files** (not Gemini foundation-model prompting). It extracts text (incl. OCR on images) and predicts labels. **[H]** ([AI classification admin help](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/label-google-drive-files-automatically-using-ai-classification))
61	- ⚠ A separate **Gemini prompt-based classification** (admin writes prompts, no training files) was announced **Nov 2025 in CLOSED BETA**. ([Workspace Updates 2025-11](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/11/gemini-data-classification-google-drive.html)) Don't assume it's GA — version-dependent for a Sept 2026 plan.
62	
63	## Licensing (broader than "Enterprise Plus only")
64	Included with **Frontline Plus** and **Enterprise Plus**, plus the **Gemini Enterprise-Legacy / Gemini Education Premium** add-ons and the **AI Security add-on**. **[H]** (admin help). The **AI Security add-on** (launched Apr 2024) is the path to AI classification for orgs not on Enterprise/Frontline Plus, though Google's AI-classification page does not enumerate exactly which base editions the add-on attaches to — the specific "reaches Business Standard/Plus" detail is **unverified [L]**. Add-on pricing is **not public** (contact sales). ([AI Security add-on](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2024/04/ai-security-add-on-google-workspace.html)). Enterprise Plus list price ~$35/user/mo annual; Enterprise Standard ~$27 (no native AI classification). **[M]** ([Workspace pricing](https://workspace.google.com/enterprise/))
65	
66	## Label constraint
67	AI classification trains on **one field per label** with **2–7 options**, published. ⚠ Two Google pages disagree on whether that field can be a badge list or **options list only** — the dedicated create-labels page says options-list only; treat that as the safer assumption. **[M]**
68	
69	## Training process (this drives timeline)
70	- Designate **labelers**; they manually apply a **training label** (must differ from the classification label) to **≥100 files per option** (a hard threshold). Google also recommends **≥500 characters per file** for best results (a best-practice guideline, not a hard block). More than 100/option is better. **[H]**
71	- System checks readiness ~24h after labeling; a **training run takes 4–6 hours** (longer for big datasets). **[H]**
72	- Model gets a **recall score**: **<50% = not ready; 50–80% = limited; >80% = ready.** Auto-apply allowed at ≥50% but Google recommends ≥80% on all options. **[H]**
73	- After enabling auto-apply: **existing** files scanned within **1–2 weeks**; new/modified files on upload/edit. **Retrains every 2 weeks** (on-demand retraining added Jul 2025). Up to **5 models/org**. **[H]** ([Jul 2025 update](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/07/google-drive-ai-classification-updates-multi-model-support-on-demand-model-training.html))
74	- ⚠ If the last eligible license lapses, the **model is deleted** (existing labels persist). **[H]**
75	
76	## Privacy & accuracy
77	- **Privacy**: models are **customer-specific, trained only on data you designate, never used for other customers or Google's public models.** **[H]** ([Roche case study](https://workspace.google.com/blog/customer-stories/roche-protects-files-ai-classification-google-drive)); general Workspace AI privacy commitments at the [Privacy Hub](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/gemini/generative-ai-in-google-workspace-privacy-hub). **[H]**
78	- **Accuracy**: Google exposes **recall** (not precision/false-positive rate). High recall at the auto-apply gate can still mean real false positives on sensitive content — a reason to keep a human-override path. **[H for the metric gap]**. The official white paper (workspace.google.com/learning/content/gws-ai-classification-whitepaper) exists but wouldn't render for the researchers — **read it yourself if you want the architecture/accuracy detail. [L on its contents]**
79	
80	**Implication for the work test:** AI classification carries a licensing cost, a multi-week training dependency (≥100 files/option + a ≥80% recall gate), false-positive risk, and a single-simple-field constraint. That's why the strong answer keeps it **off the critical path to January** — manual + default + DLP first; AI classification as a Phase-2 fast-follow on the existing backlog.
81	
82	# Part 3 — How data-classification rollouts are actually run (best practices)
83	
84	## Taxonomy: keep it small (3–5 tiers)
85	Universal consensus is **3–5 tiers**; canonical set: **Public / Internal (or "General") / Confidential / Highly Confidential.** Microsoft recommends ≤5 top-level labels (≤25 incl. sublabels) to keep adoption manageable. **[H]** ([MS data classification & labels](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-data-classification-and-labels); [MS create a framework](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework)). Varonis: "overly complex schemes create confusion and dilute adoption." **[H]** ([Varonis](https://www.varonis.com/blog/data-classification)). Use "Confidential" vs "Highly Confidential" (not adjacent "Confidential"/"Restricted") so the hierarchy is self-evident. NIST SP 800-60 uses Low/Moderate/High but is about **system categorization**, not document labeling — don't over-map it. **[H/M]** ([NIST SP 800-60r2 draft](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/60/r2/iwd))
86	- Real anecdote worth borrowing: Microsoft's internal pilot renamed "Personal" → "Non-business" and "Internal" → "General" after user confusion. Taxonomy names carry behavior; pilot and iterate. **[H]** ([MS get started with sensitivity labels](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/get-started-with-sensitivity-labels))
87	
88	## Phased rollout (crawl-walk-run)
89	0. **Discovery/plan** (≈weeks 1–4): cross-functional team, data inventory, taxonomy + per-tier controls, regulatory alignment, exec sign-off.
90	1. **Pilot** (10–50 users across IT/Legal/Compliance + one business unit): manual labeling, **no enforcement**, gather feedback, tune names/tooltips/false-positives.
91	2. **Expanded rollout + auto-labeling** (months 3–6): wave by department, enable DLP/default for well-understood data, broaden training.
92	3. **Full adoption + enforcement** (months 6–12+): mandatory labeling, advanced automation (AI classifiers), audit/compliance validation.
93	4. **Monitor/optimize** (ongoing): ≥annual taxonomy review, KPI tracking.
94	**[H]** (MS Purview guidance; [AIS regulated-environment rollout](https://www.ais.com/implementing-sensitivity-labels-in-a-highly-regulated-environment/); [Gravity Union rollout tips](https://www.gravityunion.com/blog/purview-sensitivity-labels-rollout-tips))
95	
96	## Timelines
97	- Enterprise M365 core deployment ~**12–20 weeks** (consultancy estimate). **[M]** ([EPC Group](https://www.epcgroup.net/blog/microsoft-purview-information-protection-guide))
98	- General range **3–12 months** depending on data volume, repositories, regulation, change-management maturity. **[H]**
99	(For the test's Sept 2026 → Jan 2027 window ≈ 4 months: realistic for pilot + phased manual/DLP rollout; **not** enough to lean on AI-model maturity.)
100	
101	## Change management is the real work
102	- **"~50% of an Information Protection project is business-focused, not technical."** Under-investing here is the #1 failure mode. **[H]** (MS assurance docs)
103	- **Executive sponsorship is non-negotiable** — projects without a named senior sponsor stall. **[H]**
104	- **Minimize user burden** — if labeling is tedious, users stop doing it. Automate the routine; let humans handle exceptions/overrides. **[H]**
105	- **Training**: fold into existing security-awareness training; use departmental champions; in-app tooltips + a "learn more" link. **[H]**
106	- **Role-specific messaging** beats generic announcements (legal → "compliance risk"; analysts → "faster discovery"). **[M]** ([First San Francisco Partners](https://www.firstsanfranciscopartners.com/blog/change-managements-vital-role-in-a-data-management-initiative/))
107	
108	## Manual vs. automated (the hybrid everyone lands on)
109	1. **Default** baseline label on new files (no friction, nothing unlabeled).
110	2. **DLP** for clearly-detectable regulated data (SSNs, PCI, PHI) — near-zero false positives.
111	3. **AI/trainable classifiers** for ambiguous unstructured content (contracts, IP) — higher false-positive rate, needs tuning.
112	4. **Manual override** for users to raise/adjust; block downgrades without justification.
113	**[H]** (Varonis; [Material Security on Google Drive](https://material.security/workspace-resources/google-drive-data-classification-strategies-to-protect-your-files); Gravity Union). Manual-only "leads to inconsistency, label-skipping, and apathy" and doesn't scale. **[H]**
114	
115	## Governance ownership (not IT alone)
116	Standard split: **Data Owner** (business leader, accountable, approves exceptions) / **Data Steward** (Compliance/Info-Gov, maintains taxonomy + standard) / **Data Custodian** (IT/Security, implements controls). A **steering committee** (Legal, Privacy, Compliance, IT, Comms, Records) owns the taxonomy. SANS explicitly warns against IT unilaterally defining protection needs. **[H]** ([data owner/steward/custodian](https://thedatagovernor.com/data-steward-vs-data-owner-vs-data-custodian/); [Netwrix info-governance guide](https://netwrix.com/en/resources/guides/information-governance-data-discovery-classification/); [SANS 846](https://www.sans.org/white-papers/846))
117	
118	## Common pitfalls (all **[H]** unless noted)
119	Label sprawl / too many tiers · over-classification (everyone picks "Highly Confidential" → DLP false-positive flood) · treating it as one-time vs. ongoing · no exec buy-in · org-wide launch with no pilot · tech without training · premature blanket encryption (breaks workflows) · ignoring email/PDF/chat · manual-only · vague tier names · no governance authority.
120	
121	## Success metrics
122	% files/users labeled (coverage) · classification accuracy (target 90–95%+, **[M]** on benchmark) · adoption rate (manual vs auto ratio) · DLP hit & false-positive rate · incident reduction (lagging) · **helpdesk ticket volume on labeling** (leading friction signal — should fall after training) · audit outcomes · label-distribution skew (>50% "Highly Confidential" = over-classification). **[H]** for metric types, **[M]** for specific targets.
123	
124	## Google Workspace vs. Microsoft Purview (context)
125	The generic principles (tiers, governance, change mgmt, phased pilot) apply to both. Google's classification tooling is **~2–3 years behind Purview in maturity**; Google labels don't natively cover access governance (who-has-access) — third-party tools (Material, Nightfall) fill that. Gmail labels hit GA Apr 2025; Gemini Drive classification was beta Nov 2025. **[H/M]** (Material Security; Workspace Updates)
126	
127	# ⚠ Where sources disagree / may be outdated (fact-check these)
128	1. **Badged labels per org**: 2021 blog "one per company" vs. current "150 incl. multiple badged." The relaxation wasn't formally announced — confirm in-console if it matters.
129	2. **AI classification field type**: admin-help page says "badge list OR options list"; create-labels page says "options list only." Assume options-list-only to be safe.
130	3. **AI Security add-on price**: not public anywhere — sales-only.
131	4. **Gemini prompt-based classification**: closed beta as of Nov 2025; GA status for a Sept 2026 scenario is unknown — flag as an assumption.
132	5. **Accuracy benchmarks (90–95%)**: practitioner consensus, not rigorous studies; Google publishes recall, not precision/false-positive rates.
133	6. **12–20 week timeline**: consultancy estimate, not an official SLA.
134	7. **Vault retention on non-date label fields**: documented for date fields; broader support unconfirmed.
135

They can be a simple tag or carry structured fields. **[H]** ([Google: get started as a labels admin](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/get-started-as-a-classification-labels-admin)). Managed in the **Label Manager** (Admin console → Security → Access and data control → Label manager, or drive.google.com/labels). **[H]** ([Workspace Updates 2024-07](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2024/07/enable-classification-labels-on-workspace-apps.html))

## Badged vs. standard labels (CORRECTED — important)
- A **badge list field** is a field type ("pick one from a list of badges") that renders the selected value as a **colored rectangle** in Docs/Sheets/Slides/Drive — a visible handling reminder. Only **one badge list field per label**. **[H]** ([Google: create classification labels](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-classification-labels-for-your-organization))
- **The old "one badged label per organization" rule has been relaxed.** Google's 2021 launch post said one per company ([Workspace Updates 2021-12](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2021/12/enhanced-content-classification.html)), but current docs say up to **150 labels per org, "including multiple badged labels."** The constraint is now one badge *field* per label, not one badged label per org. **[H, but the change was never explicitly announced — verify in your console if it matters]**
- As of a **Nov 2025** update, badge values display in Drive list/grid views (highest-ranked badged label shows; a count icon flags additional labels). **[H]** ([Workspace Updates 2025-11](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/11/data-classification-labels-visible-google-drive.html))
- Admins can attach a **"learn more" documentation link** to a badge field; users see it on hover or in the Labels pane. **[H]** (create-labels page above)

## Editions (who can do what)
- **Create + manually apply labels**: Frontline Starter/Standard/Plus, Business Standard/Plus, all Enterprise editions, Education Standard/Plus, Essentials tiers. **Excluded**: Business Starter, Education Fundamentals (for manual apply). **[H]** (get-started page)
- **DLP-driven auto-labeling**: requires Frontline Standard/Plus, **Enterprise Standard/Plus**, Education Fundamentals/Standard/Plus, Enterprise Essentials Plus (+ Cloud Identity Premium). **Business Standard/Plus can create and manually apply labels but CANNOT auto-apply them via DLP.** **[H]** ([Google: DLP for Drive rules](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-dlp-for-drive-rules-and-custom-content-detectors))
- **AI classification**: see Part 2.

## Limits (verbatim from Google docs) **[H]**
| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Labels per org | 150 (incl. badged) |
| Fields per label | 10 |
| Options per field | 200 |
| Labels a *user* can apply to one file | 5 |
| Total labels on a file (user + rule-applied) | 20 |
| Total labels on a Gmail message | 20 |
| Text field length | 100 chars |
| AI classification models per org | 5 |
Source: [create-labels](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-classification-labels-for-your-organization) + [get-started](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/get-started-as-a-classification-labels-admin). **Field types are immutable after publishing.**

## The three ways labels get applied
1. **Manual** — user right-clicks a Drive file → Labels → Apply (or File → Labels in Docs). Bulk apply up to 100 files. Needs edit access + "can apply" permission. **[H]** ([apply labels in Drive](https://support.google.com/drive/answer/13495216))
2. **Default classification** — auto-applies a label to **new** files (or on ownership change) scoped to an OU/group. **Does NOT retroactively label existing files. Only supports labels with an options-list field** (not badge/text/number/date/person). **[H]** ([default classification](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/apply-default-classification-labels-to-new-files-automatically))
3. **Rule-based (DLP)** and **AI classification** — see below.

## DLP integration, sharing controls, locking, retention
- **DLP auto-labeling**: a DLP-for-Drive rule scans content (predefined detectors for SSNs/credit cards/etc., custom word lists, regex, likelihood thresholds) and, on match, applies a label + a single-select options value. DLP label actions support **single-select options list fields only**. **[H]** (DLP-for-Drive page above)
- **Label-driven sharing controls**: a DLP rule's actions can **block external sharing** and **disable download/print/copy** (for commenters/viewers; editors unaffected) alongside applying a label. **[H]**
  - ⚠ Side effect: once any sharing-blocking DLP rule is active, external users can't view version history of **any** file that ever had **any** DLP rule applied — including label-only rules. **[H]** ([DLP for Drive FAQ](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/dlp-for-drive-faq))
  - There's no confirmed mechanism for a label to restrict sharing **on its own** without a DLP rule. **[L]**
- **Label locking**: labels/fields/options used by an active DLP, Vault retention, default-classification, or AI rule are **locked** — can't be disabled or deleted (renaming and adding options still allowed). Unlock by removing from all rules. **[H]** (create-labels + DLP pages)
- **Vault retention**: retention rules can key off a label's **date field** (since Jun 2023); litigation holds override retention. **[H]** ([Vault Drive retention](https://support.google.com/vault/answer/4388708)); whether non-date field values can trigger retention is **[M]**.
- **Audit**: Drive audit logs record label/DLP events (e.g. "DLP Rule applied Label Contract"); DLP rules support **"audit only"** mode for testing; the Security Investigation Tool inspects rule triggers. **[H]**

## Priority order when methods conflict (CORRECTED — it's 5 levels, not 3)
Verbatim hierarchy, highest wins: **(1) DLP without user-overwrite → (2) manual/user-applied → (3) DLP with user-overwrite → (4) AI classification → (5) default classification.** **[H]** ([AI classification page](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/label-google-drive-files-automatically-using-ai-classification)). Plain version: DLP beats AI beats default; manual user labels beat AI. Multi-DLP-rule ties break by **options-list order** (higher option wins), not rule number. **[H]**

# Part 2 — Google's AI classification for Drive labels

## What it actually is (key nuance)
The **generally-available** "AI classification" uses **custom models trained on YOUR org's own labeled files** (not Gemini foundation-model prompting). It extracts text (incl. OCR on images) and predicts labels. **[H]** ([AI classification admin help](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/label-google-drive-files-automatically-using-ai-classification))
- ⚠ A separate **Gemini prompt-based classification** (admin writes prompts, no training files) was announced **Nov 2025 in CLOSED BETA**. ([Workspace Updates 2025-11](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/11/gemini-data-classification-google-drive.html)) Don't assume it's GA — version-dependent for a Sept 2026 plan.

## Licensing (broader than "Enterprise Plus only")
Included with **Frontline Plus** and **Enterprise Plus**, plus the **Gemini Enterprise-Legacy / Gemini Education Premium** add-ons and the **AI Security add-on**. **[H]** (admin help). The **AI Security add-on** (launched Apr 2024) is the path to AI classification for orgs not on Enterprise/Frontline Plus, though Google's AI-classification page does not enumerate exactly which base editions the add-on attaches to — the specific "reaches Business Standard/Plus" detail is **unverified [L]**. Add-on pricing is **not public** (contact sales). ([AI Security add-on](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2024/04/ai-security-add-on-google-workspace.html)). Enterprise Plus list price ~$35/user/mo annual; Enterprise Standard ~$27 (no native AI classification). **[M]** ([Workspace pricing](https://workspace.google.com/enterprise/))

## Label constraint
AI classification trains on **one field per label** with **2–7 options**, published. ⚠ Two Google pages disagree on whether that field can be a badge list or **options list only** — the dedicated create-labels page says options-list only; treat that as the safer assumption. **[M]**

## Training process (this drives timeline)
- Designate **labelers**; they manually apply a **training label** (must differ from the classification label) to **≥100 files per option** (a hard threshold). Google also recommends **≥500 characters per file** for best results (a best-practice guideline, not a hard block). More than 100/option is better. **[H]**
- System checks readiness ~24h after labeling; a **training run takes 4–6 hours** (longer for big datasets). **[H]**
- Model gets a **recall score**: **<50% = not ready; 50–80% = limited; >80% = ready.** Auto-apply allowed at ≥50% but Google recommends ≥80% on all options. **[H]**
- After enabling auto-apply: **existing** files scanned within **1–2 weeks**; new/modified files on upload/edit. **Retrains every 2 weeks** (on-demand retraining added Jul 2025). Up to **5 models/org**. **[H]** ([Jul 2025 update](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/07/google-drive-ai-classification-updates-multi-model-support-on-demand-model-training.html))
- ⚠ If the last eligible license lapses, the **model is deleted** (existing labels persist). **[H]**

## Privacy & accuracy
- **Privacy**: models are **customer-specific, trained only on data you designate, never used for other customers or Google's public models.** **[H]** ([Roche case study](https://workspace.google.com/blog/customer-stories/roche-protects-files-ai-classification-google-drive)); general Workspace AI privacy commitments at the [Privacy Hub](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/gemini/generative-ai-in-google-workspace-privacy-hub). **[H]**
- **Accuracy**: Google exposes **recall** (not precision/false-positive rate). High recall at the auto-apply gate can still mean real false positives on sensitive content — a reason to keep a human-override path. **[H for the metric gap]**. The official white paper (workspace.google.com/learning/content/gws-ai-classification-whitepaper) exists but wouldn't render for the researchers — **read it yourself if you want the architecture/accuracy detail. [L on its contents]**

**Implication for the work test:** AI classification carries a licensing cost, a multi-week training dependency (≥100 files/option + a ≥80% recall gate), false-positive risk, and a single-simple-field constraint. That's why the strong answer keeps it **off the critical path to January** — manual + default + DLP first; AI classification as a Phase-2 fast-follow on the existing backlog.

# Part 3 — How data-classification rollouts are actually run (best practices)

## Taxonomy: keep it small (3–5 tiers)
Universal consensus is **3–5 tiers**; canonical set: **Public / Internal (or "General") / Confidential / Highly Confidential.** Microsoft recommends ≤5 top-level labels (≤25 incl. sublabels) to keep adoption manageable. **[H]** ([MS data classification & labels](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-data-classification-and-labels); [MS create a framework](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework)). Varonis: "overly complex schemes create confusion and dilute adoption." **[H]** ([Varonis](https://www.varonis.com/blog/data-classification)). Use "Confidential" vs "Highly Confidential" (not adjacent "Confidential"/"Restricted") so the hierarchy is self-evident. NIST SP 800-60 uses Low/Moderate/High but is about **system categorization**, not document labeling — don't over-map it. **[H/M]** ([NIST SP 800-60r2 draft](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/60/r2/iwd))
- Real anecdote worth borrowing: Microsoft's internal pilot renamed "Personal" → "Non-business" and "Internal" → "General" after user confusion. Taxonomy names carry behavior; pilot and iterate. **[H]** ([MS get started with sensitivity labels](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/get-started-with-sensitivity-labels))

## Phased rollout (crawl-walk-run)
0. **Discovery/plan** (≈weeks 1–4): cross-functional team, data inventory, taxonomy + per-tier controls, regulatory alignment, exec sign-off.
1. **Pilot** (10–50 users across IT/Legal/Compliance + one business unit): manual labeling, **no enforcement**, gather feedback, tune names/tooltips/false-positives.
2. **Expanded rollout + auto-labeling** (months 3–6): wave by department, enable DLP/default for well-understood data, broaden training.
3. **Full adoption + enforcement** (months 6–12+): mandatory labeling, advanced automation (AI classifiers), audit/compliance validation.
4. **Monitor/optimize** (ongoing): ≥annual taxonomy review, KPI tracking.
**[H]** (MS Purview guidance; [AIS regulated-environment rollout](https://www.ais.com/implementing-sensitivity-labels-in-a-highly-regulated-environment/); [Gravity Union rollout tips](https://www.gravityunion.com/blog/purview-sensitivity-labels-rollout-tips))

## Timelines
- Enterprise M365 core deployment ~**12–20 weeks** (consultancy estimate). **[M]** ([EPC Group](https://www.epcgroup.net/blog/microsoft-purview-information-protection-guide))
- General range **3–12 months** depending on data volume, repositories, regulation, change-management maturity. **[H]**
(For the test's Sept 2026 → Jan 2027 window ≈ 4 months: realistic for pilot + phased manual/DLP rollout; **not** enough to lean on AI-model maturity.)

## Change management is the real work
- **"~50% of an Information Protection project is business-focused, not technical."** Under-investing here is the #1 failure mode. **[H]** (MS assurance docs)
- **Executive sponsorship is non-negotiable** — projects without a named senior sponsor stall. **[H]**
- **Minimize user burden** — if labeling is tedious, users stop doing it. Automate the routine; let humans handle exceptions/overrides. **[H]**
- **Training**: fold into existing security-awareness training; use departmental champions; in-app tooltips + a "learn more" link. **[H]**
- **Role-specific messaging** beats generic announcements (legal → "compliance risk"; analysts → "faster discovery"). **[M]** ([First San Francisco Partners](https://www.firstsanfranciscopartners.com/blog/change-managements-vital-role-in-a-data-management-initiative/))

## Manual vs. automated (the hybrid everyone lands on)
1. **Default** baseline label on new files (no friction, nothing unlabeled).
2. **DLP** for clearly-detectable regulated data (SSNs, PCI, PHI) — near-zero false positives.
3. **AI/trainable classifiers** for ambiguous unstructured content (contracts, IP) — higher false-positive rate, needs tuning.
4. **Manual override** for users to raise/adjust; block downgrades without justification.
**[H]** (Varonis; [Material Security on Google Drive](https://material.security/workspace-resources/google-drive-data-classification-strategies-to-protect-your-files); Gravity Union). Manual-only "leads to inconsistency, label-skipping, and apathy" and doesn't scale. **[H]**

## Governance ownership (not IT alone)
Standard split: **Data Owner** (business leader, accountable, approves exceptions) / **Data Steward** (Compliance/Info-Gov, maintains taxonomy + standard) / **Data Custodian** (IT/Security, implements controls). A **steering committee** (Legal, Privacy, Compliance, IT, Comms, Records) owns the taxonomy. SANS explicitly warns against IT unilaterally defining protection needs. **[H]** ([data owner/steward/custodian](https://thedatagovernor.com/data-steward-vs-data-owner-vs-data-custodian/); [Netwrix info-governance guide](https://netwrix.com/en/resources/guides/information-governance-data-discovery-classification/); [SANS 846](https://www.sans.org/white-papers/846))

## Common pitfalls (all **[H]** unless noted)
Label sprawl / too many tiers · over-classification (everyone picks "Highly Confidential" → DLP false-positive flood) · treating it as one-time vs. ongoing · no exec buy-in · org-wide launch with no pilot · tech without training · premature blanket encryption (breaks workflows) · ignoring email/PDF/chat · manual-only · vague tier names · no governance authority.

## Success metrics
% files/users labeled (coverage) · classification accuracy (target 90–95%+, **[M]** on benchmark) · adoption rate (manual vs auto ratio) · DLP hit & false-positive rate · incident reduction (lagging) · **helpdesk ticket volume on labeling** (leading friction signal — should fall after training) · audit outcomes · label-distribution skew (>50% "Highly Confidential" = over-classification). **[H]** for metric types, **[M]** for specific targets.

## Google Workspace vs. Microsoft Purview (context)
The generic principles (tiers, governance, change mgmt, phased pilot) apply to both. Google's classification tooling is **~2–3 years behind Purview in maturity**; Google labels don't natively cover access governance (who-has-access) — third-party tools (Material, Nightfall) fill that. Gmail labels hit GA Apr 2025; Gemini Drive classification was beta Nov 2025. **[H/M]** (Material Security; Workspace Updates)

# ⚠ Where sources disagree / may be outdated (fact-check these)
1. **Badged labels per org**: 2021 blog "one per company" vs. current "150 incl. multiple badged." The relaxation wasn't formally announced — confirm in-console if it matters.
2. **AI classification field type**: admin-help page says "badge list OR options list"; create-labels page says "options list only." Assume options-list-only to be safe.
3. **AI Security add-on price**: not public anywhere — sales-only.
4. **Gemini prompt-based classification**: closed beta as of Nov 2025; GA status for a Sept 2026 scenario is unknown — flag as an assumption.
5. **Accuracy benchmarks (90–95%)**: practitioner consensus, not rigorous studies; Google publishes recall, not precision/false-positive rates.
6. **12–20 week timeline**: consultancy estimate, not an official SLA.
7. **Vault retention on non-date label fields**: documented for date fields; broader support unconfirmed.

Hi Alex,
 
Thanks for your interest in joining the IT team at Coefficient Giving and for submitting your application! We were impressed with your application and are interested in exploring your candidacy further. We would now like to invite you to the next stage, an initial interview and a paid work test.
 
Work Test Information
You will have 5 hours to complete the test, including the time spent reading the instructions. Please submit what you have, even if incomplete, if you've spent 5 hours on this test. Please submit by Monday, June 8th at 11:59pm EST. If you need more time, please let me know in advance. The work test submission page and instructions can be found in the link below.
 
https://you.ashbyhq.com/coefficientgiving/assignment/2ea60a68-c611-4660-8b1e-64a573abad15
 
We aim to grade all work tests blindly and provide an honorarium in recognition of the time taken to complete them. Upon completing the test, you will receive an honorarium of $300. In order to receive the honorarium, please fill out this form after you submit your test, selecting how you would prefer to receive payment.
 
Initial Interview
Please also schedule a 25-minute interview with me, to take place after you submit your work test, between June 8–19th (inclusive). The aim of this interview is to learn more about you, your experience, and your interest in Coefficient Giving and the role. There's nothing specific you need to do to prepare, but you may go through this brief document to learn more about us, as a portion of our time will be devoted to your questions.
 
You can schedule the interview with me here. If you're unable to find a suitable time, please do reach out and let me know!
 
Next steps
I also wanted to share an outline of the remaining stages of the process:
  • We aim to grade work tests and reach out by June 24th.
  • We will invite shortlisted candidates to an interview with Luke Willey, who this role will report to.
  • A final round of interviews (2-3) with Coefficient team members, along with reference checks, likely in early July.
  • We aim to make an offer by late July.
Feel free to reach out to me if you have any questions and please do keep us in the loop if anything changes on your end (e.g. if you receive a competing offer or have a hard deadline) and we will be happy to discuss, and do our best to expedite a decision if we can.
 
Best,
Xaviera

Work Test Information
You will have 5 hours to complete the test, including the time spent reading the instructions. Please submit what you have, even if incomplete, if you've spent 5 hours on this test. https://you.ashbyhq.com/coefficientgiving/assignment/2ea60a68-c611-4660-8b1e-64a573abad15
 
We aim to grade all work tests blindly and provide an honorarium in recognition of the time taken to complete them. Upon completing the test, you will receive an honorarium of $300. Initial Interview
Please also schedule a 25-minute interview with me, to take place after you submit your work test, between June 8–19th (inclusive). The aim of this interview is to learn more about you, your experience, and your interest in Coefficient Giving and the role. Next steps

  • We aim to grade work tests and reach out by June 24th.
  • We will invite shortlisted candidates to an interview with Luke Willey, who this role will report to.

Best,
Xaviera

*Work trial assignment for Coefficient Giving’s IT Associate role. Consists of a deployment plan, user guide, an email reply to a concerned user, a short note on AI use, and an addendum on assumptions.*

# 1\. Deployment Plan

**Date:** 6-8-2026**  
****Owner:** \[me\]

**Window:** September 2026 to January 2027.

## What we're doing, and why

Leadership already signed off on rolling out Google Workspace classification labels across the whole org. The point is to tighten up data security, make documents easier to manage, and keep us on the right side of our data-governance commitments. My job is to get it live by January and hand it off in a shape the org can sustain, without making operations worse in the process.

  

For context, Google gives you three ways to label files automatically, and they stack in a fixed priority order:

  

  - **Default classification (by org unit or group).** Cheap and dependable for a baseline, but it only kicks in on **new** files and ownership changes. It doesn't touch the files the org has already accumulated. Good for a clean floor going forward.
  - **DLP rules** (based on content). These hit new *and* existing files, and they win over the other two methods when they disagree. Best for the clear-cut sensitive stuff: PII, payment data, applicant records.
  - **AI classification**. It learns from examples, but it can't run until you've hand-labeled at least \~100 files per category to train it. Once trained it overrides default classification, though DLP still beats it. Best for the judgment calls a rule can't capture.

## On the AI classification feature

On AI classification: we will tentatively plan to roll it out, but not on day one. We have to do the manual labeling regardless, and that work doubles as AI's training set, so the order picks itself: default classification for a baseline, DLP for the obvious sensitive files, then AI for the ambiguous remainder once it performs satisfactorily.

## The labels themselves

Here's a simple four-tier scheme to use. Per Google’s own recommendations and best practices, I kept it short on purpose. The more options people get, the more they mislabel and the slower they adopt. The exact tiers are a placeholder; I'd want to settle them with Legal and the team leads in week one, not decide them myself.

|  |  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| \*\*Label\*\* | \*\*What it means\*\* | \*\*Examples\*\* | \*\*Intended access\*\* |
| \*\*Public\*\* | Fine to share outside the org | Published research, public job posts | Anyone with the link |
| \*\*Internal\*\* (the default) | Everyday staff information | Team docs, meeting notes | All staff |
| \*\*Confidential\*\* | Sensitive, need-to-know | Grantee and applicant data, finances, HR | Owning team plus named people |
| \*\*Restricted\*\* | Most sensitive, tightly held | Legal, security, board material | Explicit allow-list only |

## Who owns what

|  |  |  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| \*\*The work\*\* | \*\*Responsible\*\* | \*\*Accountable\*\* | \*\*Consulted\*\* | \*\*Informed\*\* |
| Taxonomy and policy | IT lead | IT lead | Legal/Compliance, team leads | Leadership |
| Technical setup (labels, DLP, AI) | Workspace admin | IT lead | External Workspace consultant | IT team |
| Labeling during the pilot | Pilot team members | Team leads | IT team | IT lead |
| Training and comms | IT team | IT lead | Team leads | All staff |
| Compliance sign-off | Compliance | Leadership sponsor | IT lead | All staff |

  

*Outside IT, this needs Legal/Compliance (tiers, regulatory scope, retention), team leaders (which data is sensitive, plus pilot validation), a leadership sponsor (for mandates and cross-team time), and Procurement (if we need to buy the AI Security add-on).*

## Timeline

|  |  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| \*\*Phase\*\* | \*\*When\*\* | \*\*The work\*\* | \*\*Lead\*\* |
| \*\*0. Discovery and design\*\* | Sept | Talk to stakeholders, inventory the data, lock the taxonomy, access model, and retention rules, agree on what success means | IT lead + Compliance |
| \*\*1. Build in a test OU\*\* | Oct | Create the labels, set up default classification and DLP rules, wire access controls, prove it all out in a sandbox org unit | Workspace admin |
| \*\*2. Pilot\*\* | late Oct to Nov | One or two pilot teams. Their manual labeling builds the training set. AI runs in evaluation mode. Collect feedback | IT lead + pilot leads |
| \*\*3. Rollout\*\* | Nov to Dec | Turn it on team by team, hand out the user guide, run short walkthroughs, get the helpdesk ready | IT team |
| \*\*4. Go-live (including AI classification if applicable)\*\* | Dec to Jan | Go-live.  | IT lead |
| \*\*5. Steady state\*\* | Jan to Feb | Run a retrospective, hand off to steady-state monitoring | IT Lead |

  

*AI classification by phase: there's nothing to do until the Phase 2 pilot produces ≥100 labeled files per tier, so it sits out Phases 0–1. Through Phases 2–3 it runs in evaluation mode only, graded on recall against the human labels without touching real files. At Phase 4 I switch it on per tier above ≥80% recall and spot-check the sensitive ones. In steady state it auto-retrains about every two weeks, with periodic audits.*

## What could go wrong

|  |  |
| :-: | :-: |
| \*\*The risk\*\* | \*\*How to handle/prevent it\*\* |
| It adds friction for teams that are already slammed | Automate the bulk of it (default + DLP), keep manual labeling to a one-click dropdown on a small set of files, roll out in phases, and structure the pilot so we're learning from the way they work, not teaching them a new way. |
| Mislabeling, especially by AI | Launch on rules and manual labels first, run AI in monitor mode before trusting it, only switch it on above an accuracy threshold, keep everything user-correctable, and audit samples |
| Labels lock once they're in a default-classification policy, so you can't edit or delete them | Finalize the taxonomy in Phase 0 \*before\* wiring it into any policy, and run changes through change control after that |
| Access controls break legitimate sharing or lock people out | Keep labeling and access enforcement separate at first, and only tighten access in Phase 4 once it's been tested in the sandbox OU |
|   | Build the training set from a spread of teams before turning anything on |

## What a good outcome looks like

  - By go-live, \~80% of active files carry a label, and almost all of that happened automatically.
  - The DLP detectors catch the sensitive categories without a pile of false positives.
  - No uptick in access or sharing incidents, and nobody gets locked out of their own files.
  - Compliance signs off, and the pilot teams tell me that their workflow remained largely unchanged.

# 2\. User Guide: File Classification Labels

## What's a classification label?

It's a little tag on a file in Google Drive that says how sensitive the file is, like **Internal** or **Confidential**. It doesn't change your folders, your filenames, or how you work day to day.

## Why you'd care

  - It keeps sensitive work in the right hands. The people who should open a file can, and the people who shouldn't, can't.
  - It makes things easier to find, since you can search and filter by label.
  - It helps keep us compliant, so almost none of that effort falls to you.

## The labels at a glance

|  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: |
| \*\*Label\*\* | \*\*Use it for\*\* | \*\*Who can open it\*\* |
| \*\*Public\*\* | Anything you'd be fine sharing outside the org | Whoever you share it with |
| \*\*Internal\*\* | Your everyday work (this is the usual default) | All staff |
| \*\*Confidential\*\* | Sensitive stuff: grantee data, finances, HR | Your team, plus specific people |
| \*\*Restricted\*\* | The most sensitive material | A specific named list only |

## How to label a file, when you actually need to

Most files get labeled **automatically**. When a file does need a label from you:

1.  Open it, or right-click it in Drive.
2.  Go to **File, then Labels** (or click the label icon).
3.  Pick the label and close. That's it, a couple seconds.

## FAQ

**What if I label something wrong?** Just relabel it. Nothing breaks. 

  

**Who do I ask for help?** The IT team, at \[helpdesk support address\]

**To:** <A@coefficientgiving.org> 

**From:** <B@coefficientgiving.org> 

**Subject:** Re: Concerns Re: Data Classification

  

Hi A,

  

Thanks for reaching out, this is the kind of thing I want to hear before rollouts happen so I can make sure they are implemented smoothly.

  

Regarding the workflow worry: the guiding principle of this project is to add protection without adding work. The majority of labeling happens automatically in the background, so for most files you and your team won't do anything differently. There's no new app to open and nothing changes about how you make, name, or organize files. Your current setup stays exactly as it is. The labels just sit alongside your folders, they don't replace them.

  

For the small slice of files that do need a label by hand, it's one dropdown in a menu you already use, a few seconds, and we'll only ask when the automation isn't confident enough to call it on its own.

  

On the learning curve and your team's bandwidth: I hear you, and I really don't want this being one more thing on an overburdened team. Two offers: first, we're rolling out in phases, and I'd genuinely love to have your team in an early pilot so we can tune it around how you actually work. Second, the training is a one-page guide and a short walkthrough that I would be happy to personally offer you and anyone on your team.

  

Could we schedule a 20 minute call this week? I'd like to hear what's working in your current system so we can keep it and build around it rather than over it.

  

Thanks again for flagging this early.

  

Best, B

# 4\. A Note on How I Used AI

I used Claude (Anthropic's Opus 4.8) through Claude Code, mostly as a research and drafting partner. I used it in three ways:

  

1.  First, research. Since I have only administered a Microsoft environment before, I had it use a customized **/deep-research** skill on Google Workspace file classification labels. This skill requires it to link citations for all claims, and passes a dedicated verification agent over it to mitigate hallucinations. While this process ran, I read your recommended links in the assignment (and a few extra levels deep) so I would have a basic foundation that would allow me to sanity-check what Claude said.
2.  Second, structure: I bounced the phasing, the ownership table, and the risk list off it to find gaps. I had it look for any known best practices for rollouts of these features, known failure modes, and existing guides.
3.  Third, drafting: I gave it the brief, the synthesis of our combined research, Coefficient Giving's operating values, and my own outline and calls so it had context for providing feedback. Then I had it produce critiques of my technical claims, voice, and formatting choices. The actual decisions are mine: the layered approach, holding AI classification back to a watched pilot, and how I'd answer the worried colleague.

# 5\. Assumptions

I'm writing without your real context, so I made the following assumptions:

  

  - **Workspace edition.** Since the question was asked in the assignment document, I assumed we're on a tier that supports labels, DLP, and AI classification. If we're not, the plan shrinks to default classification plus manual labeling, and the AI phase falls away.

  - **Regulatory scope.** I assumed at least PII and financial sensitivity, and possibly cross-border data for international grantees. Heavier obligations would mean pulling Legal in sooner and leaning harder on DLP.

  - **Existing tooling.** I assumed there's no current labeling scheme to migrate. If there is, that's a whole extra workstream."}

# 2\. User Guide: File Classification Labels

## What's a classification label?

It's a little tag on a file in Google Drive that says how sensitive the file is, like **Internal** or **Confidential**. It doesn't change your folders, your filenames, or how you work day to day.

## Why you'd care

  - It keeps sensitive work in the right hands. The people who should open a file can, and the people who shouldn't, can't.
  - It makes things easier to find, since you can search and filter by label.
  - It helps keep us compliant, so almost none of that effort falls to you.

## The labels at a glance

|  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: |
| \*\*Label\*\* | \*\*Use it for\*\* | \*\*Who can open it\*\* |
| \*\*Public\*\* | Anything you'd be fine sharing outside the org | Whoever you share it with |
| \*\*Internal\*\* | Your everyday work (this is the usual default) | All staff |
| \*\*Confidential\*\* | Sensitive stuff: grantee data, finances, HR | Your team, plus specific people |
| \*\*Restricted\*\* | The most sensitive material | A specific named list only |

## How to label a file, when you actually need to

Most files get labeled **automatically**. When a file does need a label from you:

1.  Open it, or right-click it in Drive.
2.  Go to **File, then Labels** (or click the label icon).
3.  Pick the label and close. That's it, a couple seconds.

## FAQ

**Do I have to reorganize my files?** Nope. Your folders and names stay exactly as they are. 

  

**Is this going to slow me down?** It shouldn't. Nearly all of it is automatic, and there's no new app to learn. 

  

**What if I label something wrong?** Just relabel it. Nothing breaks.
